title: Resident Evil
composer: Makoto Tomozawa, Akari Kaida, Masami Ueda
shortDescription: Shinji Mikami's claustrophobic Spencer Mansion nightmare that established the survival horror genre through fixed camera perspectives, strict resource scarcity, and psychological dread.
historicalSignificance: Coined the term 'Survival Horror', defined the mechanical grammar of inventory conservation and environmental tension, and proved that mature cinematic horror could become a dominant global commercial genre.

editorialContent.overview: Directed by Shinji Mikami under the guidance of Capcom general manager Tokuro Fujiwara, Resident Evil (released in Japan as Biohazard on March 22, 1996) began development as an ideological reimagining of Fujiwara's 1989 Famicom horror RPG Sweet Home. Relocating a specialized police tactical squad (S.T.A.R.S.) to an eerie neoclassical mansion isolated in the Arklay Mountains outside Raccoon City, the game plunged players into a web of viral bioweapon research conducted by the pharmaceutical giant Umbrella Corporation. Resident Evil emerged as a runaway international blockbuster, selling over 5 million units across its original iterations and establishing one of the most durable multimedia franchises in interactive media history.
editorialContent.gameplayMechanics: The mechanical design of Resident Evil is defined not by overwhelming firepower, but by deliberate vulnerability and ruthless resource triage. Players choose between Chris Redfield (higher physical resilience, smaller six-slot inventory) or Jill Valentine (eight-slot inventory, lockpick access, earlier grenade launcher acquisition). Movement relies on rotational 'tank controls' relative to character orientation rather than camera orientation, reinforcing disorientation as players navigate fixed cinematic camera angles. Combat is fraught with peril: ammunition is severely constrained, healing herbs (Green, Red, Blue) must be chemically compounded, and saving progress requires discovering scarce Ink Ribbons to log entries on manual typewriters. Storage chests provide interconnected dimensional item banking, forcing constant tactical inventory management between offensive weaponry, ammunition, and progression puzzle keys.
editorialContent.technicalInnovation: Faced with the polygon budget limitations of early 3D console hardware, Mikami's team engineered a hybrid graphical pipeline: real-time rendered 3D polygonal character and creature models were composited over high-resolution, static pre-rendered 2D background paintings. This allowed the PlayStation's limited 32-bit hardware to depict lavishly detailed Victorian architectural halls, flickering candlelight, and biological gore that would have been impossible to render in full real-time 3D geometry in 1996. The famous first-person door-opening animations and stair-climbing cutscenes were an ingenious masking technique designed to conceal the PlayStation's optical CD-ROM seek times and memory buffer flushes between room loads, converting a technical hardware bottleneck into an excruciating instrument of psychological suspense.
editorialContent.culturalImpact: Resident Evil codified 'Survival Horror' as a distinct design philosophy and commercial genre, inspiring immediate industry-wide movements that birthed Silent Hill, Dino Crisis, Parasite Eve, and Fatal Frame. Its campy B-movie English voice acting ('You were almost a Jill sandwich!') and live-action cinematic prologue became legendary cultural artifacts of the early CD-ROM era. The title transformed Capcom from an arcade-centric coin-op publisher into a premier global console software titan and demonstrated that adult-oriented horror themes could achieve massive mainstream sales.
editorialContent.preservationNotes: Historical preservation must carefully separate the original 1996 PlayStation release (and its 1997 Director's Cut edition, notable for its alternate camera angles and controversial rearranged DualShock soundtrack) from the complete 2002 Nintendo GameCube ground-up remake. Archival integrity requires documenting original Japanese uncensored FMV footage (which featured Kenneth J. Sullivan's decapitated head and Chris Redfield smoking a cigarette) that was trimmed for Western localizations.
